title: Regulatory Coordination of Antisense RNA and Encoded Protein in Cell Cycle.
projectDescription: Antisense RNAs constitute a significant part of the human genome, yet their functions in key physiological processes remain poorly understood due to complexity and the lack of suitable models. Here, we report the intricate regulatory co-ordination between antisense RNA and its encoded protein involved in safeguarding the essential physiological processes during interphase and mitosis, using antisense RNA ARHGEF17-AS1 and its encoded protein, MSEP as a model system. Mechanistically, ARHGEF17-AS1 orchestrates actin-cytoskeleton organization in interphase and mitotic spindle pole integrity via the RNF10-RPS3-Twinfilin-Dynein pathway, involving monoubiquitination dependent functional switch of RPS3 during interphase to mitosis. While MSEP ensures spindle integrity through the TPX2-Aurora A pathway. Thus, our investigations provide molecular insights into how ARHGEF17-AS1 and its protein product MSEP maintain critical cell cycle stage-specific processes through unique and coordinated actions. These findings establish a compelling model for investigating the collaborative actions between antisense RNA and its encoded protein in cellular physiology.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Immunoprecipitation (IP): Approximately 20 million cells were trypsinized, washed with cold PBS, and lysed in buffer with protease inhibitors. After a 20-minute rotation, the lysate was centrifuged, and the supernatant was pre-cleared with Protein G magnetic beads. The cleared supernatant was incubated overnight with Flag antibody-conjugated beads to capture the protein complex.  CHOP-MS: Approximately 80 million HeLa cells were used per pull-down reaction. Cells were trypsinized, washed, UV-crosslinked at 250 mJ, and lysed in a swelling buffer. After DNase treatment and lysis, chromatin was isolated, sonicated, and hybridized with LacZ or ARHGEF17-AS1 DNA oligos. Streptavidin magnetic beads were prepared and incubated with the hybridization mixture to capture RNA-protein complexes.  Pulldown samples were processed using a modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) method. Briefly, samples in elution buffer were reduced with 100 mM DTT (IP: 60°C, CHOP: 56°C). Samples were alkylated (IP: 20 mM iodoacetamide, CHOP: 10 mM MMTS) and digested with trypsin on 30 kDa Microcon Centrifugal Filter Units (Merck). Released peptides from the filters were either labelled with TMT 11-plex isobaric mass tagging reagents (Lot#: UH285566, Thermo Fisher Scientific), pooled to one sample and purified (IP) or proceeded directly to purifying with HiPPR™ detergent removal spin columns (Thermo Scientific) and desalted by Pierce peptide desalting spin columns (Thermo Fisher Scientific) (CHOP). The TMT pooled sample (IP) was analyzed using Orbitrap Lumos™ Tribrid™ mass spectrometer and unlabeled sample (CHOP) with QExactive HF mass spectrometer. Both instruments were interfaced with an Easy-nLC1200 liquid chromatography system (all Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 column (100 μm x 2 cm, particle size 5 μm, Thermo Fischer Scientific) and separated on an in-house packed analytical column (75 μm x 35 cm, particle size 3 μm, Reprosil-Pur C18, Dr. Maisch) at a flow rate of 300 nL/min with a 90 minutes gradient.
dataProcessingProtocol: Data was analyzed using Proteome Discoverer (IP: version 3.0, CHOP: version 2.4). Database searches were conducted against the Human SwissProt database. The precursor tolerance was set to 5 ppm, with fragment ion tolerances of 0.6 Da (IP) and 30 mmu (CHOP). Variable modifications included methionine oxidation; fixed modifications included cysteine alkylation (IP: carbamidomethylation, CHOP: methylthio). Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were validated with a strict FDR of 1%, and proteins were filtered at 5% FDR. Quantification for IP used TMT reporter ions with normalized intensities.
